message_source_quote: beating the white-bear baseline (0.686, which I reproduced exactly)
writeup_source_quote: White-bear (Tomasz's draft, `papers/raman2026`) reproduces at 0.686 @ push 20; this direction (cosine 0.76 with it) is weaker there but peaks higher (0.784 @ 36.5).

differences.what: Explicit characterization of the relationship as the same underlying circuit as white-bear
differences.message_quote: the direction is cos 0.76 with white-bear — same circuit, different (task-free) construction. It *is* a re-derivation in part
differences.writeup_quote: this direction (cosine 0.76 with it) is weaker there but peaks higher (0.784 @ 36.5).

differences.what: Attribution of the push/partial-alignment mechanism explanation to the source paper
differences.message_quote: Partial alignment is destructive (cos 0.5–0.6 → 0.03–0.10): the readout only survives a push that is well-aligned with the circuit. This is why generic steering vectors fail here — it's not just dose, it's axis specificity.
differences.writeup_quote: Mechanism (as in WBS): the push must exceed the natural variance along the direction; the gain is computed by L25–29, not read back; partial alignment (cos 0.5–0.6) destroys it.

rationale: Both documents credit the same source (Tomasz's draft / white-bear, papers/raman2026) as the only other reproducing direction, report the same 0.686 baseline and 0.76 cosine overlap, and both flag that framing against the draft needs coordination with Tomasz, treating the new method as partly overlapping and partly novel (task-free derivation, cross-pool robustness, axis map, dose/band structure). The message states the overlap slightly more bluntly ("same circuit," "re-derivation in part") than the write-up's more measured phrasing, and conversely omits the write-up's explicit note that the push/alignment mechanism matches the source's own account ("Mechanism (as in WBS)"), instead presenting that mechanism finding as its own screen result.
